cards.title: Match search intent before writing anything
cards.summary: Sort target keywords by informational vs commercial intent so blog posts and service pages get pointed at the right query type.
cards.use_when: Product selection and content planning: deciding which keywords get a blog post, which get a landing/service page, and which to skip entirely.
steps: Classify each keyword by the results Google already shows for it. Searches like 'buy Nike shoes' return ecommerce listings, so that intent is transactional; a query like 'how much does a plumber cost' returns explanatory pages, so that intent is informational. The source calls this out as the reason not every search is equal.
Point informational keywords at blog posts, where the visitor is researching and can be captured higher in the funnel, then brought back later.
Point transactional/money keywords at service or landing pages built to make the visitor fill out a form or buy.

Skip keywords where the top results are other businesses, directory listings, branded names, or job-seeker queries. The source walks through examples like a competitor's company name and an industry mascot and rejects them because the searcher is not a prospective customer.
For ecommerce: build category and product landing pages for buy-intent queries, and blog content for problem/research queries that feed those pages via internal links.
Verify current SERP layouts in a keyword tool or by searching, since result composition changes over time.
caveats: The intent distinction is drawn from what Google currently ranks, not from the words alone, so re-check periodically.
Source is a services example (plumbing); ecommerce mapping above is the transferable application, not a demonstrated result.

cards.title: Filter keywords by difficulty and volume
cards.summary: Use an outside SEO tool to filter a root keyword down to terms with low difficulty and real search volume before committing content budget.
cards.use_when: Keyword research for blog posts, category pages or service pages where you need a shortlist worth producing.
steps: Do not ask the AI model to invent keywords. The source says a bare request like 'give me 20 keywords for plumbing' returns a guess with no difficulty or volume data, which is the wrong starting point.
Use a standalone SEO tool's keyword tool (the source uses SEMrush's keyword magic tool; verify the current interface and pricing) and enter a root keyword to generate variations containing that root.

Filter to keyword difficulty of 30 or below. The source says low-difficulty terms (its example is difficulty two out of ten) are ones a single blog post can plausibly rank for quickly, and that this has happened for it multiple times.
Filter to a minimum monthly volume of at least 100. The source rejects keywords with only a couple of searches a month as not worth ranking for.
Sweep the filtered list manually and discard branded terms, competitor business names and unrelated matches before saving.
Work toward a list of a few hundred to a couple thousand keywords, then export it to feed the content pipeline.
Use the tool's questions tab for long-tail 'how much does X cost' style queries, and mine competitor domains for keywords they rank on.
caveats: Difficulty scoring and search volumes are third-party estimates, not Google-published numbers; treat the 30 difficulty and 100 volume thresholds as the source's heuristics, not validated cutoffs.
Aim for a few hundred to a couple thousand keywords rather than an enormous list; the source says you only need hundreds to thousands to be effective.

cards.title: Build adjacent top-of-funnel topics to capture future buyers
cards.summary: Add keywords for the wider audience that will need your product later, not just the people ready to buy now.
cards.use_when: Content planning and acquisition: filling out the top of the funnel so prospects who are not yet shopping return to you when they are.
steps: Identify the audience that will eventually buy your offer, then list what they research before that moment. The source's example is a plumbing company writing about tankless water heaters and signs you need a new water heater, which captures prospects before they are ready to hire anyone.

Map these adjacent topics to a funnel position: the source treats buy-intent queries as the bottom of a funnel and says you should also have content covering all the traffic above that point to get attention and a foot in the door.
Produce blog content for the adjacent topics and interlink it to the money pages so authority flows to pages that convert.
For ecommerce, use this for consideration-stage queries about categories and use cases (e.g. comparisons or buying guides) that link to the product and category pages you actually sell from.
Use a keyword tool's questions tab to source these adjacent topics when a niche's money keywords are thin.
Track whether adjacent-topic content later converts visitors to money pages rather than judging it on immediate conversion.
caveats: The source's example is a local service business; translating this to ecommerce is a suggested application, not a demonstrated outcome.
Adjacent content does not convert directly — the source frames it as capturing attention for later, so measure it on assisted paths.

cards.title: Build keyword clusters so one page ranks for many queries
cards.summary: Give each page one root keyword plus a cluster of related terms so a single page can surface for dozens of queries.
cards.use_when: Producing a blog post, category page or landing page where you want maximum search coverage from one piece of content.
steps: Choose one primary/root keyword for the page. The source's example root is 'how to unclog a drain'.

Assemble a cluster around it: variations such as unclog kitchen sink, unclog bathroom sink, drain won't drain, slow drain sink, home remedy clogged drain, what dissolves hair in drain. The source says pull cluster terms from your exported keyword file or have the model propose them.
Put the primary keyword in the first 100 words of the page so the page's topic is unambiguous.
Keep the cluster topically tight — the source's logic is that the cluster should let one page rank for many related searches, so don't bolt on unrelated queries.
In ecommerce, apply this to category and landing pages: one root commercial keyword plus its close variants from your keyword export, with the root keyword appearing near the top of the page copy.
Expect a page to rank for many queries you never explicitly targeted, and treat the cluster as a way to maximize that opportunity.
caveats: The source describes cluster members as secondary and tertiary keywords on the same page; over-stuffing unrelated terms undermines topical focus.
The exact number of cluster terms is not established by the source.

cards.title: Reverse-engineer the top-ranking pages into a template
cards.summary: Analyze the top non-forum results for a keyword, average their structure, and use that as the target format for your page.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting a page where you want to match what already ranks before adding your own differentiation.
steps: Identify the top three blog results for the keyword, excluding community and forum results such as Reddit, as the source does.
Have your AI agent analyze all three and extract measurable structure: average word count, average number of H2 headings, image counts, and the subtopics each post covers.
Use the averages as the target spec for your draft — the source calls this the winning formula and sets word count, headings and images from the average.
Make this analysis a mandatory pre-step before writing: the source's prompt forces the model to check the live SERP and steal what works before it drafts.
Add your own differentiators (voice, examples, original data) on top of the averaged structure rather than copying the winners' content.
For ecommerce, run the same process against category or buying-guide queries to set the required depth of your PDP or guide before writing copy.
caveats: The source's premise is that SEO is a black box — nobody outside Google knows the real weighting, so mimicry of top results is a heuristic, not a guaranteed ranking mechanism.
Averaging structure tells you what ranks now; it does not prove causation.

cards.title: Train the AI on your voice, stories and stats before drafting
cards.summary: Feed the model reference files of your writing, humor, opinions and real business numbers so generated copy does not read as generic filler.
cards.use_when: Publishing any AI-drafted store content — product descriptions, buying guides, category or landing pages — where generic copy would hurt dwell time and trust.
steps: Diagnose the problem first: the source reads a generated paragraph starting 'in today's fast-paced world' and calls it boring AI slop nobody will read, and notes that dry technical niches make this worse.
Collect references: transcripts of calls or videos, emails you've written, social posts, or passages from writers whose style you want to emulate.
Create separate reference files for voice, humor, opinions, and stories/business stats (the source maintains voice and humor files and updates them from sample posts).

Include concrete business facts the model can inject: how many jobs you've done, how long you've been operating, real anecdotes you retell to customers. The source says to store these so the model can reuse them in posts.

Give the humor file explicit rules rather than adjectives. The source's rule is that if the first 50 words don't land a joke or a self-aware aside, rewrite them, with the tone described as a funny friend explaining something over a drink.
Re-run optimization passes with an instruction to preserve voice and style, so SEO fixes don't revert the copy to bland text.
If you have no reference material, lift a passage from a writer whose tone you like and add it explicitly as a humor or tone reference.
caveats: The source is explicit that its humor rule is its own opinion, not a universal requirement; substitute a voice rule that fits your brand and product category.
Reference files must be updated as your writing evolves, otherwise the model drifts back to generic phrasing.

cards.title: Batch a site build: pages, design reference and SOP file
cards.summary: Scaffold a structured site (homepage, blog index, service index) from a single prompt plus a design screenshot and an instruction file.
cards.use_when: Launching or restructuring a store's content architecture when you need index pages and templated landing pages fast without a developer.
steps: Create one project folder and put a single instruction markdown file at its root. Treat it like training a new hire on SOPs, behavior and formatting rules — the source uses this file to encode design references and build requirements.
Download and install the coding agent (the source uses a free desktop coding workspace with a Claude Code extension; verify current names and install steps as these change).
Prompt the agent to build only the structural pages you need: a homepage, a blog index, and a service/landing index. The source keeps this minimal on purpose.
Attach a real design reference screenshot — the source pulls one from a design inspiration site — because without a reference point the output comes out looking like generic AI output.
Confirm the build renders as static pages (see the rendering card) and open the local preview link to check it.
Add pages incrementally rather than requesting a whole sprawling site in one shot.
caveats: The source compares this to 4–5 hours of manual hosting/DNS/editing setup, which is its own time estimate, not a benchmark.
Tool names, install flows and free tiers referenced in the source may have changed — verify the current interface.

cards.title: Require static rendering so crawlers get complete HTML
cards.summary: Choose static site generation over server-side or client-side rendering so search and AI crawlers see fully rendered HTML without executing JavaScript.
cards.use_when: Technical SEO setup at site build time, when deciding how pages are rendered and whether crawlers can index them at all.
steps: Understand the three options through the source's pizza analogy: static generation is a slice already made (served instantly), server-side rendering is waiting for the pizza to cook, and client-side rendering is being handed flour and told to make it yourself.

Prioritize static site generation. The source's claim is that crawlers then find the page instantly instead of waiting for JavaScript execution, and with the worst option they may get nothing back at all.
Bake this into your project instruction file so every new page inherits static rendering by default, rather than retrofitting pages later.
Check the practical consequence: the source stresses that if Google cannot access or render the page, no amount of on-page or content work will rank it.
For an existing store, audit how key commercial pages (home, category, PDP) render before investing in content, since this gates everything downstream.
caveats: The source says rendering mode is the requirement that makes indexing possible; it does not provide performance data comparing the three modes.
Some platforms render some routes dynamically; verify per template rather than assuming the whole site is static.

cards.title: Run a Lighthouse audit and hand the report to the agent to fix
cards.summary: Loop: run Lighthouse in the browser, expand the failing audits, paste the report into the coding agent, and iterate until scores hit 100.
cards.use_when: Technical SEO remediation on a new store or landing page before launch, and whenever page speed or crawlability issues are suspected.
steps: Open Chrome DevTools (three-dot menu, more tools, developer tools), find the Lighthouse panel behind the double-arrow icon if hidden, and run the page load analysis.

Read the four scores: SEO, accessibility, best practices, and performance. The source's initial results were SEO 92, best practices 100, accessibility 96, performance 53 — it treats the 53 performance score as a page that loads slow and will be ranked lower.
Expand every failing audit tab first, including the SEO failures, so the report you copy includes the full detail.
Copy the entire report and paste it into the coding agent with the target: 100% across performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO, plus generate robots.txt and sitemap.xml.
Re-run Lighthouse after the changes. The source's second run reached 100/100/100 and 96.
If any score falls short, paste the new report back with the failing reasons and repeat until resolved — the source describes this as a back-and-forth loop until the issues are fully solved.
Use this on both blog content and commercial pages, not just the homepage.
caveats: The source's target of a 100 score every time is its own standard; a single Lighthouse run is a lab estimate and varies by run and environment.
This replaces needing to understand render-blocking requests, legacy JavaScript, LCP request discovery and network dependency trees — tasks the source says previously required coding knowledge.

cards.title: Generate sitemap and robots.txt so pages can be discovered
cards.summary: Emit a sitemap listing every page and a robots file granting crawler access, because unlisted pages cannot rank regardless of content quality.
cards.use_when: Technical SEO setup or post-launch, especially after adding many blog posts or landing pages.
steps: Have the agent generate sitemap.xml covering all created pages, and robots.txt specifying what crawlers may fetch.
Open the sitemap to confirm every page you want indexed is actually listed. The source steps through its sitemap page by page to verify coverage.
Set robots.txt to allow crawling of the whole site except areas you do not want indexed — the source names admin and dashboard login pages specifically as things to exclude.
Submit the sitemap to Google so the pages get indexed; the source treats this submission step as what actually puts pages into the index.
Re-generate the sitemap whenever new pages ship so the inventory stays accurate.
Apply the same exclusion logic in ecommerce to internal search result pages, filtered URLs and account or cart paths you don't want competing in the index.
caveats: The source's rule of thumb is to allow everything except login and admin paths; the exact exclusions depend on your platform's URL structure.
Verification and submission happen in Google's own console, whose interface changes — verify current steps.

cards.title: Apply an on-page checklist without destroying the content's voice
cards.summary: Run a standardized on-page optimization pass over every page, with an explicit instruction to keep the existing tone and humor intact.
cards.use_when: Optimizing blog posts, category pages or landing pages after drafting, before publishing.
steps: Package the full checklist as a reusable prompt or file and apply it to every page, not selectively. The source maintains 80+ signals and applies them to blog posts and service pages alike.

Include in the checklist the items the source verifies after running it: 2–3 external links, 3–5 internal links, primary keyword within the first 100 words, 4–8 questions per post, and exactly one H1 heading. The source notes posts commonly carry multiple heading levels (H1, H2, H3).
Point internal links at your own related pages — the source shows the agent finding relevant posts on the site and linking to them, which passes equity to money pages.

Generate the meta title and meta description. These are invisible on the page but are the blue title and gray description shown in search results; the source confirms them by inspecting the page's head/meta tags in DevTools.

Add an explicit instruction to maintain voice, humor and style during the pass. The source warns that optimizing naively turns the copy back into dry text and that a fine balance is required, since content people actually read is what keeps them on the page.
Verify the checklist output by spot-checking several items on the rendered page rather than trusting the agent's summary.
caveats: The source's 80+ signal checklist is its own compiled list; the specific counts (2–3 external, 3–5 internal, 4–8 questions, one H1) are its conventions, not Google-published rules.
It frames on-page/technical/off-page SEO as work large competitors staff entire teams for; the checklist is a shortcut to parity, not a guarantee of ranking.

cards.title: Separate content pages from money pages and let them feed each other
cards.summary: Blog content builds topical authority that lifts the commercial pages which actually generate leads and revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to invest in content versus commercial pages, and how to structure internal linking between them.
steps: Split pages into two roles. Content pages (blog posts) exist to build topical authority and signal that you are active and trusted; money pages exist to capture buy-intent search and convert the visitor.
Feed the money pages: interlink blog posts to the commercial pages so authority and link equity flow toward the pages that convert.
Build the money pages where demand exists, using the service-plus-location (or service-plus-category) pattern, because those searchers are ready to hire or buy.
Use the source's framing that a rising domain authority lifts all pages, so content investment should be judged partly by its effect on commercial page rankings, not only on its own traffic.
Keep the two page types visually and structurally distinct in purpose, even if the commercial page reuses the homepage layout as a starting template.
For ecommerce, this maps to guides and educational content feeding category and product pages; track assisted paths into revenue, not just indexation.
caveats: The source states the domain-authority lift as its opinion, not a measured effect.
It also warns that you will not know a content strategy was wrong for years, because SEO feedback loops are slow — so the mapping between content and money pages should be deliberate from the start.

cards.title: Zip services and locations into landing pages — without overbuilding
cards.summary: Create one landing page per service-location (or service-category) pair for money keywords, kept visually consistent and deliberately limited in number.
cards.use_when: Landing page planning for a local or multi-market store that needs pages targeting '<service> <city>' style commercial queries.
steps: List the services you actually offer on one side and the locations or municipalities you serve on the other. The source's example pairs emergency plumber, drain cleaning, hot water repair and leak detector against Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal and Edmonton.
Zip them together into pages targeting each combination, since the source notes these queries follow a clear service-plus-city or city-plus-service pattern.

Source the keywords by sorting a keyword tool by cost per click — the source reasons that advertisers bidding on a term is evidence it is a money keyword, and reads the service-plus-city pattern directly out of the CPC-sorted list.
Build each landing page from a proven template: the source reuses the homepage design so every city/service page looks the same.

Do not scale this to thousands. The source says to be prudent — probably not even multiple hundreds — because service page content is inherently similar across pages, and near-duplicate pages can be a negative signal.
For ecommerce, treat category-plus-subcategory or category-plus-use-case pages as the equivalent money pages, and hold the same line on not mass-producing near-identical pages.
caveats: The source explicitly says there is no objective cap on how many service pages to build — that number is its judgment, not a metric.
The CPC figure it displays in its demo is described by the presenter as exaggerated/bad data; typical CPC in its observation is roughly $3–$20.

cards.title: Reuse your best-converting landing page across all money pages
cards.summary: Test landing page variants to find the highest-converting structure, then apply that winning template to every commercial page.
cards.use_when: Landing page and PDP optimization: choosing what layout and copy structure to standardize across commercial pages.
steps: Treat the site as a staged funnel and isolate each stage: traffic to the page, page to lead or add-to-cart, and lead to closed customer. The source says each stage has to be improved separately for maximum throughput.
Run paid traffic tests on a handful of landing page variants rather than guessing. The source ran Google Ads against five to ten variations to see which performed best.
Identify the winner and reuse its structure as the standard for all service pages, so traffic gained through SEO lands on a page known to convert.
Keep the page visually consistent with your proven template; the source notes reusing the homepage look worked tremendously well for it.
Translate the same discipline to ecommerce PDPs and category pages: test variant templates and standardize the winner, rather than hand-designing each page differently.

Note the conversion definition carefully — one of the source's winning landing pages reached a 20% conversion rate (one in five visitors), which it describes as converting into a paying customer, so distinguish this from a lead-form conversion rate when setting targets.
caveats: The 20% figure is one case-study result from the presenter's own paid-traffic tests, not a benchmark you should assume for your store.
The source does not describe the test's traffic volume, duration or statistical significance, so treat a winner as provisional and keep testing.

cards.title: Package the whole workflow as a reusable skill
cards.summary: Encode the end-to-end content process as a repeatable command so one keyword trigger produces a fully optimized page.
cards.use_when: Scaling content production after you have proven the manual workflow on at least one page.
steps: Complete one blog post or landing page manually first so the workflow is validated before automating it.

Define a skill with an explicit input and output: pull a keyword from the keyword CSV, build the keyword cluster, draft the post, pull images via your configured image API, apply your voice/humor/style files, run the on-page checklist, and reuse the already-optimized technical template.
State the reuse rule plainly in the skill: the same page structure and technical SEO setup gets reused for every future page, rather than re-solved each time.
Start a new chat session for the skill to take effect after creating it, per the source's note to refresh.
Optionally schedule it to run on a cadence — the source mentions automating a daily run and having it skip keywords already used.
Create a parallel skill for service or landing pages, since the process differs from blog production.
Verify a few outputs manually before trusting unattended runs, since the skill inherits whatever gaps exist in your references and checklist.
caveats: Where the source found an error on a scheduled run and had to resend, expect occasional failures in automated runs and check output.
Skill syntax and scheduling capabilities depend on the current version of the coding agent — verify the interface.

cards.title: Ramp publishing volume gradually to avoid an indexing red flag
cards.summary: Increase content output on a scheduled curve rather than dumping hundreds of pages at once, because a sudden volume spike is a fast route to being penalized.
cards.use_when: Replenishment and publishing cadence decisions when scaling content or launching many pages at once.
steps: Because the automation makes mass production possible, the constraint becomes cadence rather than capability. The source warns that throwing off a thousand posts simultaneously will be noticed as a volume spike.
Ramp deliberately along the pattern the source describes: day one publish once, day two once again, day three maybe twice, day five three times, day eight four times.
Set an upper bound well below mass publishing — the source says you should probably never be posting a thousand blog posts a day and calls that an easy way to get banned.
Apply the same restraint when launching a batch of new commercial or category pages: stage the rollout instead of publishing the whole set on one day.
Monitor indexing after each step of the ramp and hold the cadence if pages are not being indexed before adding more.
caveats: The specific day-by-day ramp (1,1,2,3,4) is the source's illustrative schedule, not a validated optimum.
The source attributes the risk to Google noticing volume spikes; it does not cite a documented penalty rule, so treat the guidance as risk-avoidance rather than a hard specification.

cards.title: Treat off-page SEO as optional and risky
cards.summary: The source stopped doing link-focused off-page SEO because algorithm updates repeatedly punished the sites that relied on it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in backlink and off-site authority work versus on-site content and technical work.
steps: Understand the definition: off-page SEO is what the rest of the internet says about your business and how much trust and authority Google assigns you.

Weigh the source's lived experience rather than a rule: it says off-page work used to perform well around 2018–2020, but that on each algorithm update the people who got hurt were usually the ones doing off-page SEO, and it has seen businesses devastated by it.

Choose deliberately. The source states plainly that it does not do off-page SEO now and declines to present itself as an expert, so if you pursue it, treat it as a separate discipline requiring its own expertise.
Prefer reinvesting that effort into content quality and technical health, which the source treats as the more controllable levers for ranking.
If you do pursue it, treat it as an experiment you can afford to lose rather than a foundation of the acquisition plan.
caveats: This is the presenter's stated personal choice and admitted non-expertise, not a universal rule against off-page work.
The source's claims about past performance and update-related damage are anecdotal and undated in detail.

cards.title: Rank for search to rank in AI answers
cards.summary: The source's position is that AI search visibility follows from ordinary search visibility, because AI tools retrieve answers from search engines.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to fund a separate 'AI SEO' or LLM-visibility workstream versus strengthening core search rankings.
steps: Apply the source's reasoning: when you ask Google, ChatGPT, Perplexity or Claude a question, the tool first searches an engine, pulls the listings and serves the information back — so ranking well in search should carry over to AI answers.
Therefore invest first in the fundamentals that get you into those listings: crawlable static pages, a submitted sitemap, solid on-page optimization, and content worth staying on.
Because AI tools also digest page content, keep the voice, humor and story work in place — the source treats readable, non-generic content as the core driver of both rankings and time on page.
Prioritize commercial pages for the queries where an AI answer would name a vendor or product, since those answers are built from pages that already rank.
Treat 'AI SEO' as a label rather than a distinct playbook unless you observe specific retrieval differences in your niche.
caveats: This is the presenter's asserted equivalence, offered as an opinion ('here's my honest thoughts'), with no measurement behind it.
AI answer surfaces and their sourcing behavior change frequently; the reasoning may not hold uniformly over time.

cards.title: Optimize for content quality as the leading ranking lever
cards.summary: The source's mental model: Google profits from ads, ads need sustained attention, so Google rewards content that keeps people coming back.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing where to spend effort on a store's search program when you cannot address everything at once.
steps: Accept the constraint the source states: SEO is a black box with 200-plus rumored ranking signals and nobody outside Google knows the weighting or percentages.
Reduce it to one operating principle — reverse-engineer what Google wants. Google wants ad revenue; ad revenue needs attention; attention needs content people actually want to consume and return to.

Act on that by making every page genuinely readable: the source contrasts a generic 'in today's fast-paced world' opening against a rewritten version with personality and concrete detail, and argues the boring version loses the reader immediately.
Recognize the signals this feeds. The source lists quality and depth plus engagement behaviors such as dwell time, bounce rate, scroll depth and click-through rate as among the known signals.
Use this as the tiebreaker when choosing between more pages and better pages, or between more keyword coverage and more compelling writing.
For a store, this means product and category copy that holds attention rather than templated manufacturer text copied across every SKU.
caveats: The 'content is king' framing is the source's simplification of a genuinely opaque system, presented explicitly as such.
The engagement metrics it names are described as rumored/known signals without published weights — do not build reporting around assumed thresholds.

cards.title: Compress the whole SEO workflow into four buckets
cards.summary: Find winning keywords, then handle on-page, technical and off-page work as separate tracks, using automation to match teams you otherwise could not outstaff.
cards.use_when: Planning the scope of an SEO or organic acquisition program for a store and sequencing the work.
steps: Separate the work into the source's four buckets: (1) finding winning keywords, (2) on-page SEO — what you write on the page and how it is structured, (3) technical SEO — how the site is built, including load speed and core web vitals, and (4) off-page SEO — outside trust and authority.
Sequence keyword selection first, since the source insists not every keyword is created equal and content pointed at the wrong terms fails regardless of execution quality.

Deploy pages quickly using an AI coding agent rather than a manual CMS build: the source frames this as compressing 4–5 hours of hosting, DNS and editing setup into seconds, and says one person with the agent can do the daily work of a division-sized SEO team.
Keep the on-page and technical tracks both active — the source calls them two sides of the same coin and applies the optimization checklist to both blog posts and service pages, on every page.
Deprioritize off-page work per the source's own practice, and reinvest that effort into content and technical execution.
Account for the feedback loop: the source warns a wrong SEO strategy may not reveal itself for two to four years, so track leading indicators rather than waiting for revenue verdicts.
caveats: The '$500k' and '50,000 clicks/month' figures are the presenter's own past results and are not transferable benchmarks.
The claim that one operator with an agent outperforms a 20-person team is the source's assertion, not a measured comparison.
